mark.does: *Bungai terung*, worn on each shoulder when a young Iban man leaves home on his journey.

text.what: *Bungai terung*, worn on each shoulder when a young Iban man leaves home on his journey.
text.story: A spiral at the centre stands for the tendril of a pumpkin plant; the mark is put on before the journey, not after it. A tattoo that anticipates rather than records.

text.what: Lines, dots, and combinations of both, arranged differently by each Chin group.
text.story: Full face, part face, all dots, vertical lines with dots, stars on cheek and forehead. Sixty sub-groups, and the design is the group's name written where nobody can mistake it.

mark.does: A tiger, a cat, a monkey, an elephant, a *nat* or a *bilu*, each sitting inside an oval frame of letters.

text.what: A tiger, a cat, a monkey, an elephant, a *nat* or a *bilu*, each sitting inside an oval frame of letters.
text.story:
Shway Yoe: each representation is surrounded by a roughly oval tracery of letters, which forms a curious and remarkably effective frame, so each animal has a setting of its own — and vacant spaces are filled the same way, the top and bottom finished with a scalloped line.

Sometimes the letters are said to carry a cabalistic meaning; ordinarily, he says, no more is claimed for them than beauty. The serious charms go elsewhere on the body, usually in vermilion.

*Inference —* the frame is what makes the leg read as cloth. A repeating field of bounded units is a textile pattern; a scene is a picture. These traditions chose the textile.

mark.does: The centipede, one of the standing Cordilleran figures, alongside snakes, eagles, ferns, rice grains and mountains.

text.what: The centipede, one of the standing Cordilleran figures, alongside snakes, eagles, ferns, rice grains and mountains.
text.story: The motifs are the motifs of the weaving and the pottery. A tattoo tradition in the Philippines is not a separate art with its own vocabulary; it is the same vocabulary applied to a person.

text.story: A figure from the epic used as a protective device, in the same family as the Burmese *bilu* and the Shan animal syllables. The figures travel; the grammar around them does not.

text.story: Michael King interviewed more than seventy women in the 1970s who had received it before 1907. Since the 1990s it has been worn by a foreign minister and a prime-time news anchor, which is a change in where the mark is allowed to be seen rather than in the mark.

mark.does: A grid of letters or numerals, read as a formula rather than as a picture.

text.what: A grid of letters or numerals, read as a formula rather than as a picture.
text.story:
The Lanna volume notes which numerals go in: **Burmese numerals**, which the Lanna call *hora* numerals and hold to be the right ones for saiyasat rites, while the Lanna numerals — *lek nai tham* — are kept for inscribing the dhamma. Two number systems, two jobs, on one page and on one body.

*Attested —* the same book says early Lanna took these beliefs from Pagan and then developed its own forms.

mark.does: Hand and arm marks referring to where the sea goddess's fingers were cut off.

text.what: Hand and arm marks referring to where the sea goddess's fingers were cut off.
text.story: Sedna's severed fingers became the sea animals. A woman without hand marks was refused the good afterlife; one without face marks went to the land of the crestfallen. The marks are a passport as much as an ornament.
